title: Open Source DocumentDB 1.0 Reaches General Availability
gist: DocumentDB 1.0, the MIT-licensed, Microsoft-originated and now Linux Foundation-hosted document database built on PostgreSQL with MongoDB wire-protocol compatibility, has reached general availability. It is positioned as a permissively licensed alternative to MongoDB's SSPL, backed by AWS, Google, Snowflake, Cockroach Labs and Yugabyte, but faces naming confusion with Amazon DocumentDB and unverified concerns about compatibility and latency versus MongoDB.

insights.claim: DocumentDB 1.0 is the first generally available release of an open source, MIT-licensed document database built on PostgreSQL that is compatible with the MongoDB wire protocol, so most MongoDB drivers, tools and queries work without changes.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A GA, drop-in MongoDB-compatible option on Postgres lowers switching costs away from MongoDB and Atlas.
insights.quote: Most MongoDB drivers, tools, and queries work without changes.
insights.locator: DocumentDB 1.0 is the first generally available release

insights.claim: DocumentDB consists of a PostgreSQL extension providing MongoDB API-compatible functionality plus a gateway translating MongoDB protocol requests into PostgreSQL calls; version 1.0 supports PostgreSQL 15–18 via container images, ships Linux packages for PostgreSQL 17 and 18, and includes a Kubernetes operator.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Running document workloads inside the Postgres ecosystem extends Postgres's role as the default general-purpose database.
insights.locator: DocumentDB consists of a PostgreSQL extension

insights.claim: DocumentDB plans separate long-term support and development tracks, with its versioning policy still under discussion.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Enterprise adoption likely waits for a defined LTS policy; watch for its finalization.
insights.locator: The project plans separate long-term support and development tracks

themes.theme: Licensing and industry backing vs MongoDB

insights.claim: Microsoft announced the DocumentDB open source project in early 2025 and it joined the Linux Foundation months later with support from AWS, Cockroach Labs, Google, Snowflake and Yugabyte.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A rare coalition of hyperscalers and database vendors standardizing on a MongoDB-compatible open alternative is a competitive headwind for MongoDB (MDB).
insights.locator: Microsoft announced the open source project early in 2025

insights.claim: DocumentDB's MIT license permits commercial use, modification and hosting without requiring disclosure of proprietary code, which the team explicitly contrasts with MongoDB's SSPL.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Permissive licensing lets cloud providers host MongoDB-compatible services freely, undermining the moat MongoDB built with SSPL.
insights.locator: DocumentDB and the MIT License: What to Know Before You Build

insights.claim: Microsoft product manager Patty Chow argues open-source document databases need multiple implementations to give developers deployment and infrastructure choice while preserving compatibility with MongoDB drivers and queries.
insights.speaker: Patty Chow
insights.so_what: The MongoDB API is being commoditized as a standard interface, shifting competition to storage/deployment layers.
insights.quote: Familiar drivers and query patterns are worth preserving.
insights.locator: With multiple open source options now on the market, Patty Chow

insights.claim: The DocumentDB name causes community confusion with Amazon DocumentDB, Azure DocumentDB and Azure Cosmos DB despite a disambiguation page, with a popular Hacker News comment urging a rename.
insights.speaker: marifjeren
insights.so_what: Brand confusion may slow adoption and muddy vendor attribution of MongoDB-compatible offerings.
insights.quote: DocumentDB is already what everybody calls Amazon DocumentDB.
insights.locator: Even if the project provides a page discussing the DocumentDB name disambiguation

insights.claim: Some practitioners report that MongoDB compatibility in FerretDB, a separate project that uses the DocumentDB extensions as its backend with its own MongoDB-compatible interface, has been far below expectations.
insights.speaker: 716green
insights.so_what: Compatibility gaps limit how much MongoDB workload can actually migrate, tempering the threat to MongoDB.
insights.quote: Compatibility between MongoDB and FerretDB has been absolutely minimal compared to what you would probably expect.
insights.locator: In a Reddit thread, some practitioners raise concerns

insights.claim: Layerbase's initial YCSB benchmark found PostgreSQL-based DocumentDB delivered 20–33% higher read throughput than FerretDB, while FerretDB had lower tail latency for updates in mixed workloads, though results were described as not conclusive.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Performance differentiation among MongoDB-compatible Postgres options is still unsettled.
insights.locator: Layerbase recently ran an initial comparison

insights.claim: An open GitHub issue reports higher query latency in DocumentDB 1.0 than MongoDB 9.0.4 across several workloads, though the results have not been independently verified.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: If confirmed, a latency gap would keep performance-sensitive workloads on native MongoDB.
insights.locator: An open GitHub issue reports higher query latency
